problem: Transformer policies for Open-Vocabulary ObjectNav (OVON) use self-attention over a context window, but performance does not improve with longer context, so they integrate history poorly under partial observability. RNNs compress history too aggressively.
motivation: OVON has semantic ambiguity and needs effective internal state updates from redundant egocentric history. Controlled experiments show that Transformer performance does not scale with context length, which motivates alternative state-update mechanisms such as linear attention.
key_idea: Use linear attention (recurrent, structured state updates) as the navigation policy backbone, and improve it with WSLA, which expands each head's state into multiple sub-states and reads them out with learnable softmax weights.
insight: With encoders and training fixed, the gains grow as the update rule becomes more structured: Linear Transformer 31.3 avg SR, DeltaNet 33.9, Gated DeltaNet 34.6, WSLA 36.4. Plain linearization barely helps, so the update rule matters more than linearity itself. Transformers do not gain from longer training context (they can degrade at l=500), while LA improves with it. The WSLA ablation shows state expansion (+0.6) and weighted readout (+1.2 more) both help. Gains are largest on long-distance episodes (+7.68 SR at 15m+).
method: Policy input: frozen SigLIP RGB and text encoders (768-d each) plus a 32-d previous-action embedding, concatenated and projected to d=512, with no pose input (DAgRL setting)

Backbone swap: a 4-layer decoder-only backbone over the last l embeddings, either a causal Transformer or linear attention with a per-head recurrent state S_t updated from (k_t, v_t) and read out by q_t
LA variants compared: Linear Transformer (kernel accumulation), DeltaNet (prediction-error write with coefficient beta), Gated DeltaNet (adds a data-dependent decay gate gamma)
WSLA state expansion: each of H=4 heads is expanded into E=4 sub-heads via linear projections of q and k, with a shared v and independent gates and states per sub-head, all using the gated delta rule
WSLA weighted readout: a learnable logit vector lambda in R^E, shared across heads and time, gives softmax weights over sub-head outputs, followed by RMSNorm and a SiLU gate
Training: DAgRL two-stage pipeline (150M-step DAgger, then 100M-step PPO), VER rollouts with rollout length equal to context length, 8 A100 GPUs, Adam at 2.5e-4

setting.backbone: Frozen SigLIP RGB/text encoders + 4-layer LA (WSLA) policy trained from scratch
setting.training_data: HM3D-OVON training episodes; DAgger 150M steps then PPO 100M steps (DAgRL pipeline); HSSD fine-tuning for 60M steps in one experiment
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB only, plus goal text and previous action (no pose/GPS/compass)
setting.action_space: discrete: move-forward, turn-left, turn-right, look-up, look-down, stop
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D-OVON; HSSD ObjectNav for transfer) plus real Unitree Go2

numbers_note: The real-world result (41/50 trials, 82% SR) is reported in the text only. The context-length scaling results are given only in a figure. The split for HSSD is not named in the paper (recorded as val).
results: WSLA reaches a 36.4 average SR on HM3D-OVON, versus 30.1 for the matched Transformer and 29.7 for DAgRL, i.e. +6.3 points. It also beats the GRU baseline (26.7) and the Gated DeltaNet variant (34.6). Gains are larger on long-distance episodes and on HSSD (+9.62 SR zero-shot, +8.33 after fine-tuning), with far lower and near-constant online FLOPs (~0.048G per action versus 3.5–42.5G for the Transformer). Real-world Go2 SR is 82% (41/50).
limitations: Only shallow (4-layer) backbones and bounded context windows were studied
Real-world evaluation is small (5 object categories, 2 start locations) with a simplified action set (no look up/down)
EALM does not beat WSLA on val-unseen SPL (8.8 vs 7.9), and the gain on val-unseen SR is small
